Newborn Care

Necrotising enterocolitis: signs, treatment and recovery

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Necrotising enterocolitis, or NEC, causes inflammation and injury in a newborn’s intestine. In severe cases, bowel tissue dies or develops a hole, allowing intestinal contents to leak into the abdomen. It is a medical emergency that needs hospital care, not a feeding problem to manage at home.

Which babies are most at risk?

NEC mainly affects premature and medically vulnerable newborns. It often develops in the first weeks after birth, but there is no fixed two-week window. Term babies can also be affected, particularly when other illnesses compromise intestinal health or blood flow.

There is no single established cause. An immature intestinal barrier, an abnormal inflammatory response, gut bacteria and problems with blood supply can interact. A difficult delivery is not a complete explanation for every case.

NEC is not simply an infection caused by bacteria in food. It can occur despite careful neonatal care, and a diagnosis should not be treated as proof that a parent caused it through feeding decisions.

Other serious newborn conditions, including those affecting circulation and sometimes an unusually high red-cell concentration, may be considered in the risk assessment. They do not establish the cause of NEC by themselves.

Changes that need immediate attention

Tell the neonatal team immediately about a newly swollen or discoloured abdomen, vomiting, blood in the stool or a marked change in feeding tolerance. Staff also watch for unusual sleepiness, temperature instability, pauses in breathing and changes in heart rate.

At home, a newborn with green vomit, a swollen painful-looking abdomen, blood in the stool or poor feeding together with lethargy needs urgent medical assessment. Do not wait for every symptom to appear or for a routine appointment.

Call emergency services if your baby is struggling to breathe, is blue or grey around the lips or tongue, becomes unresponsive or is difficult to wake. These signs can have several causes, all requiring urgent attention.

An ordinary episode of wind or spit-up does not diagnose NEC. Equally, a baby does not need a fever to be seriously unwell. Describe what has changed and when it began.

Diarrhoea may accompany feeding intolerance, although blood in the stool or a swollen abdomen has other possible causes too. The team considers the combination and progression of signs.

How the neonatal team checks for NEC

Assessment combines the baby’s condition, abdominal examination, imaging and laboratory tests. Abdominal X-rays can show characteristic gas patterns; ultrasound may provide additional information. Repeated examinations or images may be needed as the illness evolves.

Blood tests help assess infection, blood counts, clotting and the effects of illness. Blood in stool can support concern but does not establish NEC on its own. Neither a single high white-cell count nor a low platelet count is a standalone diagnosis.

Fluid normally exists within the bowel. Its presence does not prove that there is a hole. The team looks for the overall clinical and imaging evidence of injury or perforation and decides whether surgical assessment is needed.

A surgical team may occasionally place a drain into the abdominal cavity in a critically ill baby. This is different from routinely inserting a needle to look for fluid inside the intestine, and is not a standard diagnostic step for every suspected case.

Treatment gives the bowel a chance to recover

The hospital team usually pauses milk feeds while providing fluids and nutrition through a vein. A tube through the nose or mouth into the stomach can drain fluid and air. Antibiotics treat or help control infection.

Breathing support, blood-pressure support and other treatments may be needed according to the baby’s condition. Staff monitor the response closely and involve a neonatal surgeon when appropriate.

Do not independently stop feeds for a prolonged period, restart them early or substitute a different milk as treatment. Feeding changes in suspected NEC need prompt clinical supervision and a plan for hydration and nutrition.

If you are expressing milk, ask the neonatal team how to maintain your supply and store milk during the treatment period. They will guide its use when feeding can safely resume.

Some babies need surgery

A perforation, severely damaged bowel or deterioration despite medical treatment can make surgery necessary. The surgeon aims to remove tissue that cannot recover while preserving functioning intestine.

Depending on the baby’s stability and findings, treatment may involve a drain, bowel surgery or an ostomy, where bowel is brought to an opening on the abdomen. The exact approach and timing are individual decisions.

Ask what the team has found, whether a temporary stoma is expected and how nutrition will be provided. Further operations may be needed, including reconnection of the bowel when appropriate.

Recovery and follow-up

Many babies recover, but the outlook varies with prematurity, illness severity and how much intestine is affected. It is not possible to promise full recovery from the diagnosis alone.

Scar tissue can later narrow the bowel. Babies who lose a substantial length of intestine may have difficulty absorbing nutrients and need specialist nutritional support. Follow-up can include feeding, growth, development and surgical review.

After discharge, follow the team’s instructions about vomiting, abdominal swelling, stool changes and feeding difficulties. Keep the neonatal or surgical contact details available and seek urgent help for concerning changes.

Human milk can reduce NEC risk in premature babies, but no feeding method guarantees prevention. Do not add an over-the-counter probiotic to a premature baby’s feeds without the neonatal team: products and protocols differ, and live organisms can cause serious infection in vulnerable infants.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NEC is assessed from examination, imaging and laboratory findings together.

Milk feeds and nutrition must be managed by the neonatal team; deterioration may require urgent surgery.

How BeMama can help

Ask for daily explanations of feeding, imaging and surgical decisions and keep follow-up contact information after discharge.

When to seek help

Green vomiting, blood in stool, abdominal swelling with poor feeding or lethargy in a newborn needs urgent care.

Sources and further reading

  • NICHD / NIH — Necrotizing Enterocolitis

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • NEC requires urgent hospital assessment and can progress quickly.
  • Prematurity is a major risk factor, but term babies can also be affected.
  • Diagnosis uses the whole clinical picture, not one symptom or blood result.
  • Recovery may require ongoing feeding, growth and bowel follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Does every baby with NEC need an operation?

No. Some improve with bowel rest, intravenous nutrition and antibiotics. Surgery is considered when the findings or response to treatment require it.

Is NEC limited to the first two weeks?

No. Timing varies, including with gestational age and other medical conditions.

Can I prevent NEC with a probiotic?

Do not start one yourself. Neonatal units use different evidence-based protocols, and some probiotic products can cause invasive infection in premature infants.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
